blocks.text: In the middle of Anatolia, between the towns of Nevşehir, Ürgüp and Avanos, lies one of the strangest landscapes in the world. Over millions of years, eruptions of three volcanoes, Erciyes, Hasan and Göllüdağ, covered the plateau with thick layers of ash that hardened into a soft rock, tuff. Wind and water have been carving it ever since into valleys, ridges and pillars up to 40 metres high, many of them topped with a cap of harder stone: the *peri bacaları*, fairy chimneys.

The soft rock is easy to dig, and people have long cut their homes into it. From the 4th century, Christian hermits and then monks settled in the valleys, and around Göreme they carved hundreds of churches and chapels out of the rock. Churches from the period of Byzantine iconoclasm (725–842) are decorated only with simple crosses; after 842, painters covered the walls with scenes from the Bible. The Göreme Open-Air Museum brings together more than thirty of them, among them the Tokalı Church, painted in the 10th century, and the Karanlık (Dark) Church, from around 1200.

There is more below ground. The underground cities of Kaymaklı and Derinkuyu go down level after level into the rock; Derinkuyu reaches about 85 metres and could shelter thousands of people with their animals and food, behind round stone doors that rolled shut from inside. The people of the region used them as refuges in times of danger, during the Arab–Byzantine wars among others, and tunnels several kilometres long connect the two cities.

Until the 1920s many villages of the region were home to Greek-speaking Christians, who left for Greece in the population exchange of 1923 (see [the Republic](a2-u01-culture)). Derinkuyu's tunnels were rediscovered in 1963, when a resident knocked through a wall of his house.

The name itself is old: it first appears as Katpatuka in the inscriptions of the Persian kings Darius I and Xerxes, at the end of the 6th century BCE. The region was later a kingdom and then a province of the Roman Empire, and its Christian bishops, Basil of Caesarea among them, were famous in the early Church.

In 1985 UNESCO added Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia to its World Heritage List. Today, on calm mornings, dozens of hot-air balloons rise over the fairy chimneys at sunrise, and many visitors sleep in old cave houses turned into hotels.
Here are a traveller's plans, in the future tense of this unit:

blocks.tr: Yarın sabah çok erken kalkacağız. Balona bineceğiz ve güneşi göreceğiz. Sonra Göreme'de eski kiliseleri gezeceğiz. Akşam Derinkuyu'ya gideceğiz. Orada çok fotoğraf çekeceğim. Gece bir mağarada kalacağız: otelimiz bir mağara!
blocks.en: Tomorrow morning we'll get up very early. We'll go up in a balloon and watch the sun rise. Then we'll visit the old churches in Göreme. In the evening we'll go to Derinkuyu. I'll take lots of photos there. At night we'll sleep in a cave: our hotel is a cave!

sources.title: Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia
sources.note: Inscribed in 1985; erosion of volcanic tuff into pillars up to 40 m; monasticism from the 4th century; crosses only in the iconoclast period (725–842), figurative frescoes after 842; Tokalı Kilise (10th century), Karanlık Kilise (late 12th to early 13th century); Kaymaklı and Derinkuyu as refuges

sources.title: Cappadocia
sources.note: Volcanic deposits from Erciyes, Hasan and Göllüdağ; the name first recorded as Katpatuka in the inscriptions of Darius I and Xerxes; a kingdom until AD 17, then a Roman province; the Cappadocian Fathers, Basil among them; Göreme a monastic centre from 300 to 1200; more than 30 rock-cut churches in the Göreme Open Air Museum; sunrise balloon flights

sources.title: Derinkuyu underground city
sources.note: About 85 m deep; up to 20,000 people with livestock and food; rolling stone doors; rediscovered in 1963 during a house renovation; tunnels to Kaymaklı; abandoned after the Christian inhabitants left in the 1923 population exchange

sources.title: Göreme
sources.note: Fairy chimneys (peribacalar); hot-air balloon rides; old cave houses converted into hotels; Göreme National Park on the World Heritage List in 1985
